topic_title: The Supermarket Shuffle: Why Shelves Keep Moving

sources.title: Altering product placement to create a healthier layout in supermarkets: Outcomes on store sales, customer purchasing, and diet in a prospective matched controlled cluster study
sources.authors_or_organization: Vogel, C., Crozier, S., Penn-Newman, D., Ball, K., Moon, G., Lord, J., Cooper, C., Baird, J.
sources.fetched_extraction: A prospective matched controlled pilot cluster study across 6 discount supermarkets in England (3 intervention, 3 matched control), running April 2016 to March 2017 (6 months). Intervention had two parts: (1) expanding fresh fruit and vegetable sections and repositioning them near store entrances, plus relocating frozen vegetables to more prominent aisles; (2) removing confectionery from all checkouts and from aisle-end displays directly opposite checkouts, replacing them with nonfood items and water. Findings: fresh fruit and vegetable sales rose by 1.71 standard deviations at 3 months (95% CI 0.45-2.96, P=0.01), equivalent to approximately 6,170 extra portions per store per week, and by 2.42 SDs at 6 months (95% CI 0.22-4.62, P=0.03), approximately 9,820 extra portions per store per week. Confectionery sales fell by 1.05 SDs at 3 months (95% CI -1.98 to -0.12, P=0.03), approximately 1,359 fewer portions per store per week, and by 1.37 SDs at 6 months (95% CI -2.95 to 0.22, P=0.09, not statistically significant), approximately 1,575 fewer portions per store per week. No significant impact was detected on overall total store sales in any period. Among 150 women aged 18-45 recruited to a linked purchasing/diet survey (62 intervention, 88 control; 8% attrition at 3 months, 14% at 6 months), women's self-reported diet quality improved at 3 months in intervention stores, adjusted for area-level deprivation (IMD) (beta=0.29 SDs); a further analysis adjusting for all confounders gave beta=0.26 SDs, P=0.06 (not reaching conventional significance, described by the authors as a useful signal rather than definitive proof). Fruit/vegetable purchasing increased in intervention households while decreasing in control households; confectionery purchasing showed no significant intervention effect. Effect sizes for fruit/vegetable and confectionery sales (the 1.71/2.42 and 1.05/1.37 SD figures above) are model-based estimated differences between the intervention stores' observed trajectory and a counterfactual prediction of what those stores would have done absent the intervention, not simple raw arithmetic differences between intervention and control store sales.

sources.title: Exploring the Impact of Supermarket Store Layout and Atmospheric Elements on Consumer Behavior: A Field Research Study in Greece
sources.authors_or_organization: Mantratzis, P., Tsiotras, G., Tsironis, L.K., Gotzamani, K.
sources.journal_or_venue: Journal of Operations and Strategic Planning (SAGE / International Management Institute, Kolkata)
sources.fetched_extraction: A field research study of 205 participants in Greece assessing shopper perceptions and attitudes toward supermarket layout and atmospheric elements (building design, customer traffic patterns, merchandise arrangement, spatial proximity). The study reports that retail environment characteristics impact shoppers' emotional reactions, which in turn influence impulse buying behavior, and that store atmosphere and layout design significantly influence consumer decision-making, perception of the store, and satisfaction. Note: only abstract/summary-level detail was accessible via direct fetch; full-text methodology and effect-size figures were not retrievable.

sources.title: Strategic Rearrangement of Retail Shelf Space Allocations: Using Data Insights to Encourage Impulse Buying
sources.fetched_extraction: Proposes a dynamic shelf allocation-relocation method for retailers to periodically rearrange storewide product placement over time, using association rule mining and optimization-based heuristics to identify highly affine and profitable product pairs, then optimizing which departments sit in which aisles and how space within each aisle is allocated. The explicit purpose of the periodic rearrangement scheme is to maximize impulse buying: the paper reports that this strategic, data-driven rearrangement approach consistently outperforms both simple visual/manual rearrangement of shelf space and several existing shelf-allocation techniques that rely on multi-level association rule mining, in terms of the resulting impulse-purchase uplift. NOTE: this extraction is based on the paper abstract as summarized by a search engine result, not a full-text fetch (the publisher page returned 403 Forbidden on direct fetch); no further methodological detail (sample size, specific percentage uplift) beyond this abstract-level summary was retrievable. CLARIFICATION: this is a methods/data-evaluation study (using transaction data and simulation/optimization to evaluate the proposed allocation algorithm), not a report of a live in-store deployment or field experiment. Also note: while the DOI and early-view record are dated 2022, the formal journal publication (Expert Systems with Applications, Volume 216) is dated 2023; when citing a year, either is defensible but should be described precisely (e.g. "a 2022/2023 study" or specify DOI-year vs print-year) rather than asserted as a single unambiguous publication year.

sources.title: Why Grocery Stores Regularly Rearrange Their Layouts (And Why It Works)
sources.authors_or_organization: The Global Display Solution (retail display trade publication)
sources.fetched_extraction: A retail-display trade publication describing general industry practice: grocery stores regularly and continuously rearrange their layouts. States four general business reasons, without citing statistics or named studies: (1) novelty -- rearranging creates a sense of novelty that draws customers, even regular shoppers, to explore the store when it looks different; (2) impulse purchases -- strategic rearrangement encourages impulse buying, described as a key revenue generator for grocery stores; (3) navigation -- better layouts optimize traffic flow and ease of navigation; (4) seasonal promotions -- stores rearrange layouts to showcase seasonal promotions and sales, boosting visibility. NOTE: this source gives NO concrete frequency data (no monthly/quarterly/seasonal cadence figures) and cites no underlying studies or statistics of its own; it should be treated as general industry-practice background only (TERTIARY_AGGREGATOR tier), not as a source for any specific number or dated claim.
